meta.title: SLATE research: cooking, recipes and alcohol
meta.rules: Every figure carries a source URL. null means not found in a usable source; nothing is invented. Values marked "from search summary" were read from a search-engine summary of the page because the page itself refused the fetch (403); treat them as lower confidence.
meta.recipeFieldNotes: Quantities in g, ml or ct (count); tsp = 5 ml, tbsp = 15 ml, 1 cup = 240 ml, 1 oz = 28.35 g, 1 lb = 453.6 g. quantity null means the page gave no amount (pinch, handful); the page wording is in original. cuisine and vegetarian are compiler labels, not stated by the sources. methodSummary is written fresh, not copied. keepsInFridgeDays defaults to FoodSafety.gov 3-4 days for cooked dishes when the recipe page is silent.
blockedSources: nhtsa.gov PDFs (403, used mirrors or search excerpts)

weekdayVsWeekend.note: from search summary of Table 2; not fetched directly

atusFoodPrepAndCleanup.note: BLS American Time Use Survey, Table 1. 'Food preparation and cleanup' combines cooking, food presentation and kitchen clean-up (including washing dishes). Averages over all persons, including those who did none that day.
atusFoodPrepAndCleanup.splitPrepVsCleanupNote: ATUS publishes 'Food and drink preparation' and 'Kitchen and food clean-up' separately in its detailed A-1 tables, but those tables could not be retrieved (bls.gov/tus/tables pages returned only the landing page). Not found; do not invent a split.

dishwashing.handWashingNote: No government per-load hand-washing time was found. The only official time figure is ENERGY STAR's annual saving below.
dishwashing.energyStarTimeSavedNote: ENERGY STAR: using a certified dishwasher 'can save you over 230 hours of personal time over the course of a year' compared with hand washing ("almost 10 days").
dishwashing.energyStarEnergyVsHand: less than half as much energy as washing by hand
dishwashing.standardCapacityDefinition: more than eight place settings and six serving pieces
dishwashing.dishwasherCycleNote: ENERGY STAR materials do not state a cycle duration; not found in an official source.

homeCookingFrequency.source: U.S. EIA, Today in Energy, 15 Aug 2022 (2020 RECS)

microwave.source: U.S. EIA, Today in Energy (2015 RECS)

applianceEnergy.note: Typical ranges from commercial energy sites (EnergySage, Direct Energy), not a government measurement; treat as estimates. The DOE Energy Saver appliance-wattage page returned 404. kWh per hour of use equals kW drawn while the element is on; ovens cycle their element, so real kWh per hour is below the rated wattage.
applianceEnergy.annualCookingKwhNote: A search summary attributed 290 kWh (electric cooktop) and 660 kWh (gas cooktop) per household for 2020 to RECS, but the EIA page fetched states no kWh, so this is left null.

standardDrinks.examples: 12 fl oz regular beer ~5%; 8-9 fl oz malt liquor ~7%; 5 fl oz table wine ~12%; 1.5 fl oz distilled spirits ~40%

standardDrinks.name: unit
standardDrinks.examples: 175 ml glass of 12% wine = 2.1 units; 25 ml single 40% spirit = 1 unit; 35 ml = 1.4 units; pint of strong lager = 3 units, lower-strength lager just over 2

widmark.formula: C = (A / (r * W)) - beta * t  where C = BAC, A = grams ethanol absorbed, W = body mass, r = Widmark factor, beta = elimination rate, t = hours since drinking began

rSource.citation: Posey D, Mozayani A. The estimation of blood alcohol concentration: Widmark revisited. Forensic Sci Med Pathol 2007;3:33-39 (reporting Widmark's original values)

eliminationRates.label: NHTSA average for moderate drinkers
eliminationRates.source: NHTSA, Computing a BAC Estimate, Oct 1994

eliminationRates.label: NHTSA 'above average': heavy drinkers (60+ drinks per month)
NHTSA 'below average' conservative figure (fewer than 20% of population this slow)

widmark.populationRangeNHTSA: below 0.010 to above 0.040 g/dL per hour
widmark.elimination0015Note: The 0.015 g/dL/h figure is widely used by BAC calculators and is attributed to Jones (2010, Forensic Sci Int 200:1-20), but the primary text could not be retrieved, so it is not cited as verified. Verified figures are 0.017 (NHTSA average) and 0.018 (Widmark).

nhtsaBodyWaterMethod.note: NHTSA 1994 method (from Moskowitz, Appendix I of the 1992 Report to Congress): BAC (g/100 ml) = grams ethanol / (kg body mass * water fraction * 1000) * 0.806 * 100, minus metabolism counted from the start of drinking. NHTSA notes body-water percentage is not the same as Widmark's r. Worked example: 128 lb male, one 12 oz 4.5% beer gives peak 0.030; after 1 h at 0.012/h, 0.018.

widmark.bacUnits: US BAC is g per 100 ml blood (or per 210 L breath); 0.08 = 80 mg/100 ml = 0.8 g/L. UK/IE breath limits are in micrograms per 100 ml breath; Mexico City breath limit in mg per litre of breath.

Sale or supply to under-18s prohibited (Intoxicating Liquor Act 1988); exception in a private residence with parental consent

nhtsa.source: NHTSA, The ABCs of BAC (DOT HS 809 844) / NHTSA drunk-driving page; text from search excerpts (PDF returned 403)

bands.typical: some loss of judgment; relaxation, slight body warmth, altered mood
bands.driving: decline in visual functions (rapid tracking of a moving target); decline in ability to perform two tasks at the same time (divided attention)

bands.typical: exaggerated behavior, may have loss of small-muscle control (e.g., focusing eyes), impaired judgment, usually good feeling, lowered alertness, release of inhibition
bands.driving: reduced coordination, reduced ability to track moving objects, difficulty steering, reduced response to emergency driving situations

bands.typical: muscle coordination becomes poor (balance, speech, vision, reaction time, hearing); harder to detect danger; judgment, self-control, reasoning and memory impaired
bands.driving: concentration, short-term memory loss, speed control, reduced information processing (signal detection, visual search), impaired perception

bands.typical: clear deterioration of reaction time and control, slurred speech, poor coordination, slowed thinking
bands.driving: reduced ability to maintain lane position and brake appropriately

bands.typical: far less muscle control than normal, vomiting may occur (unless high tolerance), major loss of balance
bands.driving: substantial impairment in vehicle control, attention to driving task, and necessary visual and auditory information processing

niaaa.source: NIAAA, Understanding the Dangers of Alcohol Overdose (updated Apr 2021)

bands.label: Mild impairment
effects: mild speech, memory, attention, coordination, balance impairments
perceived beneficial effects such as relaxation

bands.label: Increased impairment
effects: perceived benefits give way to increasing intoxication
increased risk of aggression in some people
speech, memory, attention, coordination, balance further impaired
significant impairments in all driving skills
increased risk of injury to self and others

bands.label: Severe impairment
effects: speech, memory, coordination, attention, reaction time, balance significantly impaired
vomiting and other signs of alcohol overdose common

bands.label: Life threatening
effects: significant risk of death in most drinkers due to suppression of vital life functions

niaaa.bingeDefinition: pattern bringing BAC to 0.08 g/dL or higher, typically 4 drinks (women) or 5 drinks (men) in about 2 hours
niaaa.highIntensityDefinition: two or more times the binge thresholds
overdoseSigns: slow breathing (fewer than 8 breaths per minute)
irregular breathing (10 seconds or more between breaths)
extremely low body temperature, bluish skin or paleness
niaaa.bacKeepsRising: BAC can continue to rise after drinking stops or the person is unconscious.

hangover.peaksWhen: symptoms are worst when BAC returns to about zero
hangover.performance: attention, decision-making and muscle coordination can be impaired; driving, operating machinery or caring for others can be affected

sleep.niaaa: people fall asleep faster after drinking but sleep is fragmented and they wake earlier

review.citation: Ebrahim IO, Shapiro CM, Williams AJ, Fenwick PB. Alcohol and sleep I: effects on normal sleep. Alcohol Clin Exp Res 2013;37(4):539-549
findings: at all doses, reduced sleep onset latency, more consolidated first half of sleep, more disruption in second half
first-half REM reduction significant at high doses; total-night REM % decreased at moderate and high doses
slow-wave sleep increased in first half of night
review.caveat: The review's methods were criticised (Pressman et al. 2015, Alcohol Clin Exp Res).

primary.citation: Compton RP, Berning A. Drug and Alcohol Crash Risk. NHTSA Traffic Safety Facts Research Note DOT HS 812 117, Feb 2015 (Virginia Beach case-control study; Lacey et al.)
primary.measure: relative risk of police-reported crash involvement vs BrAC 0.00, Table 8
primary.comparisonToBlomberg: At 0.04 this model gives 1.60 vs 1.00 in Blomberg; at 0.10, 5.64 vs 2.66 in Blomberg; mostly within Blomberg's 95% CIs.

blomberg.citation: Blomberg RD, Peck RC, Moskowitz H, Burns M, Fiorentino D. The Long Beach/Fort Lauderdale relative risk study. J Safety Res 2009;40:285-292 (final report 2005)
blomberg.note: Full table not retrieved. Values stated in NHTSA 812 117: RR 1.00 at 0.04 and 2.66 at 0.10. Secondary summaries (UNC School of Government) say nearly 3x at 0.08, ~20x at 0.15, 80x at 0.20 - not verified against the paper.

crashRiskByBac.druid: DRUID pooled EU analysis (via NHTSA 812 117): BAC 0.08-0.12 = 5-30x; above 0.12 = 20-200x sober risk.
crashRiskByBac.grandRapids: Borkenstein et al. 1964 (Grand Rapids Study) first established the BAC-crash risk relationship; numeric table not retrieved.
